sections.h2: Selling a house in Sahuarita, AZ
sections.html:
In Sahuarita you can hire an agent, handle the sale yourself, or accept a cash offer that needs no mortgage. Your timeline and the condition of the house usually settle the question. Family homes dominate here, and owners live in 81.0 percent of occupied houses.

  • Agent listing: get the house ready, open it for showings and wait out the buyer's loan.
  • Sale by owner: pick the price, meet buyers and draft the deed and affidavit on your own.
  • Cash sale: no bank is involved, so measure the offer against what a listing would net after repairs and fees.

Get the terms in writing whichever way you go, and check the permit points below before you sign.

The town lies in Pima County, roughly 15 miles south of Tucson. An estimated 37,694 people lived here as of July 1, 2025, a 10.6 percent rise over the 2020 base. For 2020 to 2024 the median owner-occupied home was worth $364,300, rent ran $1,837 and household income was $104,680, with 2.89 people per household.

Those medians cover the whole town and are only a rough yardstick for an offer. Commutes average 28.6 minutes, and the Sun Shuttle between Sahuarita and Tucson runs weekdays only, so a buyer who works in Tucson will weigh the drive.

Planned communities come up often with buyers, since their rules and fees differ from a plain subdivision. Rancho Sahuarita and its resort are in the north, Quail Creek is in the southeast and Madera Highlands is in the south.

Sahuarita Unified School District covers most of the town, with a portion in the Continental Elementary School District. District lines cut across the town boundary, so the district itself has to confirm the schools for an exact address. Families look at this first. Put the district name in your listing or offer packet, and tell buyers who to call to verify it.

Inspections tend to turn up two things: work done without a permit and open complaints. Community Development covers building and zoning compliance. Weeds, junk vehicles and illegal signs fall to Planning and Zoning, while a structure built without a permit, or one that is substandard or dangerous, falls to Building Safety. File a complaint on the Accela Citizen Access portal, in person or at (520) 822-8852.

The general rule is that alterations, replacements and repairs need a permit. Small jobs are the exception:

ProjectExempt from a building permit up to
One-story detached shed200 square feet, with no plumbing, electrical or mechanical work
Masonry wall6 feet high
Wood, vinyl or wrought iron fence7 feet high
Retaining wall4 feet high
Deck not attached to the house200 square feet and no more than 30 inches above grade

Private concrete paths and driveways, painting, tile, carpet and cabinet replacement are also exempt. A room addition, a patio enclosure or new wiring belongs with the Building Safety Division at 520-822-8866. If you added something without a permit, call before you list, so the answer shapes your price rather than surprising you in escrow.

sections.h2: What to do about unpermitted work
sections.html:
Most buyers do not mind a shed or a fence. They mind surprises. Built something that needed a permit and never got one? You can ask Building Safety what it would take to permit it today, or you can disclose it and sell the house as is. The second path tends to lower offers or steer the sale toward cash.

Take photos of the work, find any receipts from the contractor and write down the year it was done. If the work involved wiring or plumbing, say so, because buyers and inspectors treat those differently from a painted fence. A short, honest summary handed over early builds more trust than a clever explanation given late.

Open complaints matter too. If a neighbor reported weeds, a junk vehicle or a sign, clear the problem first and keep proof of the fix. The Community Development Department can tell you whether a complaint is still open on your address.

An association adds a step to every sale. Call its manager the day you decide to sell and request the governing documents and a statement of dues owed. Any unpaid balance gets settled at closing, and an unknown figure can stall the deed.

Ask whether it restricts rentals, fences, sheds or exterior changes. Buyers will, and the answer can shift the price. Keep the paperwork in the same folder as your tax bill and deed so the title company can pick it up in one place.

sections.h2: Recording the deed in Pima County
sections.html:
Recording any document with the Pima County Recorder costs a flat $30 under A.R.S. 11-475. Sending a document in by mail adds a $1 processing fee, and getting back one that was submitted in error costs $5. Payment is by cash, check or money order, plus Visa or Mastercard if you pay in person. Pick up the affidavit of property value form from the Arizona Department of Revenue.

A.R.S. 11-1133 makes that affidavit part of any deed that changes title. Buyer and seller, or their agents, sign it, and it lists the price, the parcel number and the sale date. An incomplete affidavit with no exemption notation gets the deed refused. Ask the Pima County Treasurer for the current tax bill, since closing figures depend on it.

Request the current tax bill from the Pima County Treasurer before you accept a contract. The title company needs it to divide the year's tax between you and the buyer, and any unpaid amount comes out of your proceeds at closing. If you are unsure whether something is owed, the Treasurer can give you a balance for your parcel.

When the settlement statement arrives, read each line. It should show the recording fee, any HOA charges, payoffs on loans and your net proceeds. A figure that surprises you is easier to question before you sign than after the deed is recorded.

1. Pick a route and request offers in writing.
  2. Get HOA documents and a dues statement if you are in a planned community.
  3. Call the Building Safety Division about any work done without a permit.
  4. Pull your tax bill from the Treasurer.
  5. Open escrow so title can draft the deed and affidavit.
  6. Recording happens in Pima County, and your proceeds follow.

A cash sale removes the buyer's loan approval. Permit questions, HOA paperwork and recording remain, and they decide how fast you can actually close.

faqs.q: What does it cost to record a deed in Pima County?
faqs.a: Thirty dollars for any document, plus a $1 fee if you mail it in. The Arizona Department of Revenue supplies the affidavit of property value form.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit for a shed or fence in Sahuarita?
faqs.a: Not always. A one-story detached shed up to 200 square feet with no utilities, a masonry wall up to 6 feet and a fence up to 7 feet are exempt. Larger projects, or any with plumbing or electrical work, need a permit.
Most of the town is in Sahuarita Unified School District, with a portion in the Continental Elementary School District. Confirm the assignment for your address with the district.

faqs.q: How many people live in Sahuarita?
faqs.a: An estimated 37,694 as of July 1, 2025. The 2020 census counted 34,134 and the 2010 census counted 25,259.

faqs.q: Who do I call about a code complaint in Sahuarita?
faqs.a: The Community Development Department at (520) 822-8852, or file online through Accela Citizen Access. For permit questions, the Building Safety Division is at 520-822-8866.
